headline: FCC/CISA Alert: Juice Jacking Risks at Public USB Ports
summary: The FCC and CISA warn that free public USB charging ports in airports, hotels, and cafes can be weaponized to steal data or install malware via the USB data pins—a technique known as 'juice jacking.' This carousel breaks down the attack chain, vulnerable topology, and practical hardware/software mitigations for travelers and developers.

slides.title: That Free Airport USB Port Might Be Stealing Your Data
slides.subtitle: How a simple charge can become a full device compromise
slides.body: You plug in at a public USB port to top up your phone. Unknown to you, the port's data pins are active—silently pulling photos, contacts, or installing spyware. The FCC and CISA have issued a joint warning: treat every public USB port as hostile.
slides.deep_dive: USB was designed for both power and data. A standard USB-A port has four pins: VCC (power), D- and D+ (data), and GND. When you plug into a charger, only VCC and GND should be connected. Malicious ports—or compromised charging stations—keep the data pins live, turning a power connection into a bidirectional data channel. This is 'juice jacking': the attacker's hardware negotiates a data session with your device, then exfiltrates data or pushes malware, all while your battery icon shows charging.
slides.key_fact: Public USB ports can activate data pins to access your device without any user interaction beyond plugging in.
slides.why_it_matters: Engineers and travelers routinely charge devices in airports, hotels, and conferences. A single compromised port can breach corporate credentials, 2FA tokens, or proprietary code on a developer's phone.

slides.title: What Is Juice Jacking?
slides.body: Juice jacking is a hardware-based attack where a USB charging port is modified—or a malicious cable is used—to establish a data connection with the plugged-in device. The attacker can then: (1) extract files, contacts, messages, and authentication tokens; (2) install monitoring software or persistent backdoors; (3) trigger automated backups to an attacker-controlled server. No software vulnerability on the device is required—the USB protocol itself permits this when data pins are active. FCC and CISA emphasize that any public USB port (airport kiosks, hotel lamps, rental cars) should be assumed compromised.
slides.key_fact: The attack exploits the USB specification's dual-use design for power and data, requiring zero user consent or device vulnerability.
slides.why_it_matters: This is not a theoretical risk. Demonstrations at DEF CON and Black Hat have shown complete device takeover via malicious charging stations. For engineers carrying SSH keys, API tokens, or unreleased code, the impact is immediate and severe.

slides.title: From Plug to Pwn: The Juice Jacking Kill Chain

steps.title: Physical Access & Port Preparation
steps.desc: Attacker modifies a public USB port or leaves a malicious cable. Data pins (D+, D-) are wired to a hidden controller (e.g., Raspberry Pi, USB Rubber Ducky) instead of—or in addition to—the power supply.

steps.title: Device Enumeration & Trust Establishment
steps.desc: When the victim plugs in, the device detects the data lines and enumerates as a USB peripheral. The attacker's controller speaks USB protocols (ADB, MTP, PTP, or proprietary) to negotiate a trusted data session—often without any prompt on modern OSes if USB debugging or 'trust this computer' was previously enabled.

steps.title: Data Exfiltration / Payload Delivery
steps.desc: The controller issues commands to pull databases (contacts, SMS, photos), extract authentication tokens, or push a malicious app/configuration profile. The device continues to charge, so the victim sees only a battery icon—not a data transfer indicator.

slides.key_fact: The attack completes in seconds while the user believes they are only charging.
slides.why_it_matters: Understanding each step reveals where defenses—hardware blockers, OS settings, and user habits—can break the chain.

slides.title: Where the Exploit Enters: The USB Port Boundary

nodes.name: Public USB Port
nodes.sub: VCC, GND, D+, D- all connected

nodes.name: Victim Device
nodes.sub: Phone, laptop, tablet — USB OTG / host mode

slides.body: The trust boundary is the USB port itself. In a legitimate charger, only VCC and GND cross the boundary. In a juice-jacking port, the data pins cross the boundary into an attacker-controlled controller. The device sees a standard USB host and happily enumerates. No network, no Wi-Fi, no Bluetooth—just the copper wires you plugged into.
slides.key_fact: The attack surface is the physical USB interface; no network connectivity is required.
slides.why_it_matters: Network firewalls, VPNs, and endpoint detection do not protect against a direct hardware data path. Defense must happen at the port or device configuration level.

slides.title: Why Default USB Behavior Enables Juice Jacking
before_items: Data pins active on all USB connections
No user prompt for new USB host (if previously trusted)
Charging indicator shows only power, not data activity
after_items: Hardware data blockers (USB condoms) physically disconnect D+/D-
OS setting: 'Charge only' / 'No data transfer' default for new ports
Require explicit user consent for each new USB host connection
Visible data-transfer indicator in status bar when D+/D- are active
slides.body: The root cause is a design trade-off: USB prioritizes convenience (plug-and-play data) over security. Devices assume any USB host is trustworthy once the user has approved one. Attackers exploit this by presenting a malicious host that the device treats as familiar. The fix is to invert the default: data pins off unless the user explicitly enables them for a specific, trusted connection.
slides.key_fact: USB's default 'data-on' behavior is a feature, not a bug—but it becomes a vulnerability in untrusted physical environments.
slides.why_it_matters: Developers can enforce secure defaults in custom hardware (e.g., corporate devices) and advocate for OS-level 'charge-only' modes. Travelers must carry hardware blockers.

slides.title: Perimeter Defense vs. Zero-Trust USB Architecture
left_items: Public USB port → direct data path to device
Device trusts any USB host after first approval
right_items: Hardware: USB data blocker / 'charge-only' cable (physically cuts D+/D-)
Device OS: Default 'charge-only' mode; per-host authorization required
Firmware: USB port controller enforces power-only negotiation (USB-PD without data)
Policy: Ban public USB ports for corporate devices; provide portable trusted chargers
Monitoring: Log USB enumeration events; alert on unexpected data-role swaps
slides.body: Zero-trust for USB means: never trust a port just because it delivers power. Every layer—cable, port controller, OS, policy—must independently verify that data pins are inactive unless explicitly authorized. This mirrors network zero-trust: verify explicitly, least privilege, assume breach.
slides.key_fact: A $5 USB data blocker physically severs the attack path; no software update can bypass a missing copper trace.
slides.why_it_matters: Layered defenses ensure that even if one control fails (e.g., OS bug), the hardware blocker still prevents data exfiltration.

slides.title: Immediate Actions for Travelers, Engineers & Security Teams
items: Carry a USB data blocker ('USB condom') on every trip—keep one on your keyring.
Use only your own AC charger + cable plugged into a wall outlet—never a public USB port.
Enable 'Charge only' / 'No data transfer' default in Android (Settings → USB preferences) or iOS (Lockdown Mode / USB Restricted Mode).
For corporate devices: enforce USB Restricted Mode via MDM; provision hardware data blockers.
Developers: design custom hardware with USB-PD controllers that negotiate power only (no data role) for charging ports.
Audit: run `lsusb -t` (Linux) or `system_profiler SPUSBDataType` (macOS) after charging in public to verify no data endpoints enumerated.
Rotate any credentials (SSH keys, API tokens) that were on a device charged via public USB in the last 90 days.
Report suspicious public charging stations to facility security and CISA via their incident reporting portal.
slides.key_fact: Physical data blockers are the single most effective, lowest-cost mitigation—no software required.
slides.why_it_matters: This checklist turns awareness into habit. For engineers, it protects intellectual property; for organizations, it reduces the attack surface of a ubiquitous but overlooked vector.
